chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, who said:

I entered the bathhouse with Abu Baseer, and I looked at Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him); he had waxed (his body hair) and his two armpits had been waxed with Al-Noura. So I informed Abu Baseer, and he said, 'Guide me to him so I may ask him about it.' I said, 'I have seen him.' He said, 'You have seen him, but I have not seen him' (for he was blind). 'Guide me to him.' So I guided him to him, and he said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! My guide informed me that you have waxed and waxed your armpits with Al-Noura.' He said, 'Yes, O Abu Muhammad! Plucking the armpits weakens the vision. Wax, O Abu Muhammad.' He said, 'I have waxed a few days ago.' He said, 'Wax, for it is purifying.'

key_terms.اطَّلَى: To wax (remove hair using a paste/substance)
key_terms.النُّورَةِ: Al-Noura (a specific waxing substance or paste)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between plucking and waxing armpit hair according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the Imam’s attention to personal hygiene and aesthetic grooming within the bathhouse context, distinguishing between the physical effects of plucking versus waxing. It establishes waxing as a 'purifying act' (tahoor), linking bodily cleanliness to spiritual purity, a key concept in Shia fiqh regarding minor and major ritual ablutions. The narration also reflects the scholarly practice of verifying details through trusted companions, as Abu Basir relies on the narrator's direct observation to seek the Imam's ruling.
